Chemistry
Chemistry is the scientific study of the properties and behavior of <color=#3366CC>matter</color>. It is a physical science within the <color=#3366CC>natural</color>
<color=#3366CC>sciences</color> that studies matter: composition, structure, properties, behavior and the changes they undergo during

<color=#3366CC>reactions</color> with other <color=#3366CC>substances</color>. Chemistry also addresses the nature of <color=#3366CC>chemical bonds</color> in <color=#3366CC>chemical compounds</color>.
In the scope of its subject, chemistry occupies an intermediate position between <color=#3366CC>physics</color> and <color=#3366CC>biology</color>. It is sometimes
called the central science because it provides a foundation for understanding both <color=#3366CC>basic</color> and <color=#3366CC>applied</color> scientific
disciplines at a fundamental level. For example, chemistry explains aspects of plant growth (<color=#3366CC>botany</color>), the formation of
igneous rocks (<color=#3366CC>geology</color>), how atmospheric <color=#3366CC>ozone</color> is formed and how environmental pollutants are degraded (<color=#3366CC>ecology</color>),
the properties of the soil on the Moon (<color=#3366CC>cosmochemistry</color>), how medications work (<color=#3366CC>pharmacology</color>), and how to collect
<color=#3366CC>DNA</color> evidence at a crime scene (<color=#3366CC>forensics</color>).
Chemistry has existed under various names since ancient times. It has evolved, and now chemistry encompasses
various areas of specialisation, or subdisciplines, that continue to increase in number and interrelate to create further
interdisciplinary fields of study. The applications of various fields of chemistry are used frequently for economic
purposes in the <color=#3366CC>chemical industry</color>.
Etymology
The word chemistry comes from a modification during the <color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color> of the word <color=#3366CC>alchemy</color>, which referred to an

earlier set of practices that encompassed elements of chemistry, <color=#3366CC>metallurgy</color>, <color=#3366CC>philosophy</color>, <color=#3366CC>astrology</color>, <color=#3366CC>astronomy</color>,
<color=#3366CC>mysticism</color>, and <color=#3366CC>medicine</color>. Alchemy is often associated with the quest to turn lead or other base metals into gold, though
alchemists were also interested in many of the questions of modern chemistry.
The modern word alchemy in turn is derived from the <color=#3366CC>Arabic</color> word al-kīmīā. This may have <color=#3366CC>Egyptian</color> origins since
al-kīmīā is derived from the <color=#3366CC>Ancient Greek</color>, which is in turn derived from the word <color=#3366CC>Kemet</color>, which is the ancient name of
Egypt in the Egyptian language. Alternately, al-kīmīā may derive from 'cast together'.
Modern principles
The current model of atomic structure is the <color=#3366CC>quantum mechanical model</color>. Traditional chemistry starts with the study of

<color=#3366CC>elementary particles</color>, <color=#3366CC>atoms</color>, <color=#3366CC>molecules</color>, <color=#3366CC>substances</color>, <color=#3366CC>metals</color>, <color=#3366CC>crystals</color> and other aggregates of <color=#3366CC>matter</color>. Matter can be
studied in solid, liquid, gas and plasma <color=#3366CC>states</color>, in isolation or in combination. The interactions, <color=#3366CC>reactions</color> and
transformations that are studied in chemistry are usually the result of interactions between atoms, leading to
rearrangements of the <color=#3366CC>chemical bonds</color> which hold atoms together. Such behaviors are studied in a chemistry
<color=#3366CC>laboratory</color>.
The chemistry laboratory stereotypically uses various forms of <color=#3366CC>laboratory glassware</color>. However glassware is not central
to chemistry, and a great deal of experimental (as well as applied/industrial) chemistry is done without it.
A <color=#3366CC>chemical reaction</color> is a transformation of some substances into one or more different substances. The basis of such a
chemical transformation is the rearrangement of electrons in the chemical bonds between atoms. It can be symbolically
depicted through a <color=#3366CC>chemical equation</color>, which usually involves atoms as subjects. The number of atoms on the left and
the right in the equation for a chemical transformation is equal. (When the number of atoms on either side is unequal,
the transformation is referred to as a <color=#3366CC>nuclear reaction</color> or <color=#3366CC>radioactive decay</color>.) The type of chemical reactions a
substance may undergo and the energy changes that may accompany it are constrained by certain basic rules, known
as <color=#3366CC>chemical laws</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Energy</color> and <color=#3366CC>entropy</color> considerations are invariably important in almost all chemical studies. Chemical substances are
classified in terms of their structure, phase, as well as their <color=#3366CC>chemical compositions</color>. They can be analyzed using the
tools of <color=#3366CC>chemical analysis</color>, e.g. <color=#3366CC>spectroscopy</color> and <color=#3366CC>chromatography</color>. Scientists engaged in chemical research are known
as <color=#3366CC>chemists</color>. Most chemists specialize in one or more sub-disciplines. Several <color=#3366CC>concepts</color> are essential for the study of
chemistry; some of them are:
Matter
In chemistry, matter is defined as anything that has rest mass and <color=#3366CC>volume</color> (it takes up space) and is made up of
<color=#3366CC>particles</color>. The particles that make up matter have rest mass as well – not all particles have rest mass, such as the
<color=#3366CC>photon</color>. Matter can be a pure <color=#3366CC>chemical substance</color> or a <color=#3366CC>mixture</color> of substances.
Atom
The <color=#3366CC>atom</color> is the basic unit of chemistry. It consists of a dense core called the <color=#3366CC>atomic nucleus</color> surrounded by a space
occupied by an <color=#3366CC>electron cloud</color>. The nucleus is made up of positively charged <color=#3366CC>protons</color> and uncharged <color=#3366CC>neutrons</color> (together
called <color=#3366CC>nucleons</color>), while the <color=#3366CC>electron</color> cloud consists of negatively charged <color=#3366CC>electrons</color> which orbit the nucleus. In a neutral
atom, the negatively charged electrons balance out the positive charge of the protons. The nucleus is dense; the mass
of a nucleon is approximately 1,836 times that of an electron, yet the radius of an atom is about 10,000 times that of its
nucleus.
The atom is also the smallest entity that can be envisaged to retain the chemical properties of the element, such as

<color=#3366CC>electronegativity</color>, <color=#3366CC>ionization potential</color>, preferred <color=#3366CC>oxidation state</color>(s), <color=#3366CC>coordination number</color>, and preferred types of bonds to
form (e.g., <color=#3366CC>metallic</color>, <color=#3366CC>ionic</color>, <color=#3366CC>covalent</color>).
Element
A chemical element is a pure substance which is composed of a single type of atom, characterized by its particular
number of <color=#3366CC>protons</color> in the nuclei of its atoms, known as the <color=#3366CC>atomic number</color> and represented by the symbol Z. The <color=#3366CC>mass</color>
<color=#3366CC>number</color> is the sum of the number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus. Although all the nuclei of all atoms belonging to
one element will have the same atomic number, they may not necessarily have the same mass number; atoms of an
element which have different mass numbers are known as <color=#3366CC>isotopes</color>. For example, all atoms with 6 protons in their
nuclei are atoms of the chemical element <color=#3366CC>carbon</color>, but atoms of carbon may have mass numbers of 12 or 13.
The standard presentation of the chemical elements is in the <color=#3366CC>periodic table</color>, which orders elements by atomic number.
The periodic table is arranged in <color=#3366CC>groups</color>, or columns, and <color=#3366CC>periods</color>, or rows. The periodic table is useful in identifying
<color=#3366CC>periodic trends</color>.
Compound
A compound is a pure chemical substance composed of more than one element. The properties of a compound bear
little similarity to those of its elements. The standard nomenclature of compounds is set by the <color=#3366CC>International Union of</color>
<color=#3366CC>Pure and Applied Chemistry</color> (IUPAC). <color=#3366CC>Organic compounds</color> are named according to the <color=#3366CC>organic nomenclature</color> system.
The names for <color=#3366CC>inorganic compounds</color> are created according to the <color=#3366CC>inorganic nomenclature</color> system. When a compound
has more than one component, then they are divided into two classes, the electropositive and the electronegative
components. In addition the Chemical Abstracts Service (CAS) has devised a method to index chemical substances. In
this scheme each chemical substance is identifiable by a number known as its CAS registry number.
Molecule
A molecule is the smallest indivisible portion of a pure <color=#3366CC>chemical substance</color> that has its unique set of chemical
properties, that is, its potential to undergo a certain set of chemical reactions with other substances. However, this
definition only works well for substances that are composed of molecules, which is not true of many substances (see
below). Molecules are typically a set of atoms bound together by <color=#3366CC>covalent bonds</color>, such that the structure is electrically
neutral and all valence electrons are paired with other electrons either in bonds or in lone pairs.
Thus, molecules exist as electrically neutral units, unlike ions. When this rule is broken, giving the "molecule" a charge,
the result is sometimes named a molecular ion or a polyatomic ion. However, the discrete and separate nature of the
molecular concept usually requires that molecular ions be present only in well-separated form, such as a directed beam
in a vacuum in a <color=#3366CC>mass spectrometer</color>. Charged polyatomic collections residing in solids (for example, common <color=#3366CC>sulfate</color> or
<color=#3366CC>nitrate</color> ions) are generally not considered "molecules" in chemistry. Some molecules contain one or more unpaired
electrons, creating <color=#3366CC>radicals</color>. Most radicals are comparatively reactive, but some, such as <color=#3366CC>nitric oxide</color> (NO) can be
stable.

The "inert" or <color=#3366CC>noble gas elements</color> (<color=#3366CC>helium</color>, <color=#3366CC>neon</color>, <color=#3366CC>argon</color>, <color=#3366CC>krypton</color>, <color=#3366CC>xenon</color> and <color=#3366CC>radon</color>) are composed of lone atoms as
their smallest discrete unit, but the other isolated chemical elements consist of either molecules or networks of atoms
bonded to each other in some way. Identifiable molecules compose familiar substances such as water, air, and many
organic compounds like alcohol, sugar, gasoline, and the various <color=#3366CC>pharmaceuticals</color>.
However, not all substances or chemical compounds consist of discrete molecules, and indeed most of the solid
substances that make up the solid crust, mantle, and core of the Earth are chemical compounds without molecules.
These other types of substances, such as <color=#3366CC>ionic compounds</color> and <color=#3366CC>network solids</color>, are organized in such a way as to lack
the existence of identifiable molecules per se. Instead, these substances are discussed in terms of formula units or <color=#3366CC>unit</color>
<color=#3366CC>cells</color> as the smallest repeating structure within the substance. Examples of such substances are mineral salts (such as
<color=#3366CC>table salt</color>), solids like carbon and diamond, metals, and familiar <color=#3366CC>silica</color> and <color=#3366CC>silicate minerals</color> such as quartz and granite.
One of the main characteristics of a molecule is its geometry often called its <color=#3366CC>structure</color>. While the structure of <color=#3366CC>diatomic</color>,
triatomic or tetra-atomic molecules may be trivial, (<color=#3366CC>linear</color>, angular pyramidal etc.) the structure of polyatomic molecules,
that are constituted of more than six atoms (of several elements) can be crucial for its chemical nature.
Substance and mixture
A chemical substance is a kind of matter with a definite <color=#3366CC>composition</color> and set of properties. A collection of substances is
called a mixture. Examples of mixtures are <color=#3366CC>air</color> and <color=#3366CC>alloys</color>.
Mole and amount of substance
The mole is a unit of measurement that denotes an <color=#3366CC>amount of substance</color> (also called chemical amount). One mole is
defined to contain exactly 6.02214076×10^23 particles (atoms, molecules, ions, or electrons), where the <color=#3366CC>number of</color>
<color=#3366CC>particles</color> per mole is known as the <color=#3366CC>Avogadro constant</color>. <color=#3366CC>Molar concentration</color> is the amount of a particular substance per
volume of <color=#3366CC>solution</color>, and is commonly reported in mol/dm3.
Phase
In addition to the specific chemical properties that distinguish different chemical classifications, chemicals can exist in
several phases. For the most part, the chemical classifications are independent of these bulk phase classifications;
however, some more exotic phases are incompatible with certain chemical properties. A phase is a set of states of a
chemical system that have similar bulk structural properties, over a range of conditions, such as <color=#3366CC>pressure</color> or
<color=#3366CC>temperature</color>.
Physical properties, such as <color=#3366CC>density</color> and <color=#3366CC>refractive index</color> tend to fall within values characteristic of the phase. The
phase of matter is defined by the <color=#3366CC>phase transition</color>, which is when energy put into or taken out of the system goes into
rearranging the structure of the system, instead of changing the bulk conditions.
Sometimes the distinction between phases can be continuous instead of having a discrete boundary; in this case the
matter is considered to be in a <color=#3366CC>supercritical</color> state. When three states meet based on the conditions, it is known as a
<color=#3366CC>triple point</color> and since this is invariant, it is a convenient way to define a set of conditions.
The most familiar examples of phases are <color=#3366CC>solids</color>, <color=#3366CC>liquids</color>, and <color=#3366CC>gases</color>. Many substances exhibit multiple solid phases.
For example, there are three phases of solid <color=#3366CC>iron</color> (alpha, gamma, and delta) that vary based on temperature and
pressure. A principal difference between solid phases is the <color=#3366CC>crystal structure</color>, or arrangement, of the atoms. Another
phase commonly encountered in the study of chemistry is the aqueous phase, which is the state of substances
dissolved in <color=#3366CC>aqueous solution</color> (that is, in water).
Less familiar phases include <color=#3366CC>plasmas</color>, <color=#3366CC>Bose–Einstein condensates</color> and fermionic condensates and the <color=#3366CC>paramagnetic</color>
and <color=#3366CC>ferromagnetic</color> phases of <color=#3366CC>magnetic</color> materials. While most familiar phases deal with three-dimensional systems, it is
also possible to define analogs in two-dimensional systems, which has received attention for its relevance to systems in
<color=#3366CC>biology</color>.
Bonding
Atoms sticking together in molecules or crystals are said to be bonded with one another. A chemical bond may be
visualized as the <color=#3366CC>multipole</color> balance between the positive charges in the nuclei and the negative charges oscillating
about them. More than simple attraction and repulsion, the energies and distributions characterize the availability of an
electron to bond to another atom.

The chemical bond can be a <color=#3366CC>covalent bond</color>, an <color=#3366CC>ionic bond</color>, a <color=#3366CC>hydrogen bond</color> or just because of <color=#3366CC>Van der Waals force</color>.
Each of these kinds of bonds is ascribed to some potential. These potentials create the interactions which hold atoms
together in <color=#3366CC>molecules</color> or <color=#3366CC>crystals</color>. In many simple compounds, <color=#3366CC>valence bond theory</color>, the Valence Shell Electron Pair
Repulsion model (<color=#3366CC>VSEPR</color>), and the concept of <color=#3366CC>oxidation number</color> can be used to explain molecular structure and
composition.
An ionic bond is formed when a metal loses one or more of its electrons, becoming a positively charged cation, and the
electrons are then gained by the non-metal atom, becoming a negatively charged anion. The two oppositely charged
ions attract one another, and the ionic bond is the electrostatic force of attraction between them. For example, <color=#3366CC>sodium</color>
(Na), a metal, loses one electron to become an Na+ cation while <color=#3366CC>chlorine</color> (Cl), a non-metal, gains this electron to
become <color=#3366CC>Cl</color>. The ions are held together due to electrostatic attraction, and that compound <color=#3366CC>sodium chloride</color> (NaCl), or
common table salt, is formed.
In a covalent bond, one or more pairs of <color=#3366CC>valence electrons</color> are shared by two atoms: the resulting electrically neutral
group of bonded atoms is termed a <color=#3366CC>molecule</color>. Atoms will share valence electrons in such a way as to create a <color=#3366CC>noble</color>
<color=#3366CC>gas</color> electron configuration (eight electrons in their outermost shell) for each atom. Atoms that tend to combine in such a
way that they each have eight electrons in their valence shell are said to follow the <color=#3366CC>octet rule</color>. However, some elements
like <color=#3366CC>hydrogen</color> and <color=#3366CC>lithium</color> need only two electrons in their outermost shell to attain this stable configuration; these atoms
are said to follow the duet rule, and in this way they are reaching the electron configuration of the noble gas <color=#3366CC>helium</color>,
which has two electrons in its outer shell.
Similarly, theories from <color=#3366CC>classical physics</color> can be used to predict many ionic structures. With more complicated
compounds, such as <color=#3366CC>metal complexes</color>, valence bond theory is less applicable and alternative approaches, such as the
<color=#3366CC>molecular orbital</color> theory, are generally used.
Energy
In the context of chemistry, energy is an attribute of a substance as a consequence of its <color=#3366CC>atomic</color>, <color=#3366CC>molecular</color> or
aggregate structure. Since a chemical transformation is accompanied by a change in one or more of these kinds of
structures, it is invariably accompanied by an <color=#3366CC>increase</color> or <color=#3366CC>decrease</color> of <color=#3366CC>energy</color> of the substances involved. Some energy
is transferred between the surroundings and the reactants of the reaction in the form of heat or <color=#3366CC>light</color>; thus the products
of a reaction may have more or less energy than the reactants.
A reaction is said to be exergonic if the final state is lower on the energy scale than the initial state; in the case of
endergonic reactions the situation is the reverse. A reaction is said to be <color=#3366CC>exothermic</color> if the reaction releases heat to the
surroundings; in the case of <color=#3366CC>endothermic reactions</color>, the reaction absorbs heat from the surroundings.
Chemical reactions are invariably not possible unless the reactants surmount an energy barrier known as the <color=#3366CC>activation</color>
<color=#3366CC>energy</color>. The speed of a chemical reaction (at given temperature T) is related to the activation energy E, by the
Boltzmann's population factor – that is the probability of a molecule to have energy greater than or equal to E at the
given temperature T. This exponential dependence of a reaction rate on temperature is known as the <color=#3366CC>Arrhenius</color>
<color=#3366CC>equation</color>. The activation energy necessary for a chemical reaction to occur can be in the form of heat, light, <color=#3366CC>electricity</color>
or mechanical <color=#3366CC>force</color> in the form of <color=#3366CC>ultrasound</color>.
A related concept <color=#3366CC>free energy</color>, which also incorporates entropy considerations, is a very useful means for predicting the
feasibility of a reaction and determining the state of equilibrium of a chemical reaction, in <color=#3366CC>chemical thermodynamics</color>. A
reaction is feasible only if the total change in the <color=#3366CC>Gibbs free energy</color> is negative, if it is equal to zero the chemical
reaction is said to be at <color=#3366CC>equilibrium</color>.
There exist only limited possible states of energy for electrons, atoms and molecules. These are determined by the
rules of <color=#3366CC>quantum mechanics</color>, which require <color=#3366CC>quantization</color> of energy of a bound system. The atoms/molecules in a higher
energy state are said to be excited. The molecules/atoms of substance in an excited energy state are often much more
reactive; that is, more amenable to chemical reactions.
The phase of a substance is invariably determined by its energy and the energy of its surroundings. When the
<color=#3366CC>intermolecular forces</color> of a substance are such that the energy of the surroundings is not sufficient to overcome them, it
occurs in a more ordered phase like liquid or solid as is the case with water (H2O); a liquid at room temperature
because its molecules are bound by <color=#3366CC>hydrogen bonds</color>. Whereas <color=#3366CC>hydrogen sulfide</color> (H2S) is a gas at room temperature
and standard pressure, as its molecules are bound by weaker <color=#3366CC>dipole–dipole interactions</color>.
The transfer of energy from one chemical substance to another depends on the size of energy <color=#3366CC>quanta</color> emitted from one
substance. However, heat energy is often transferred more easily from almost any substance to another because the
<color=#3366CC>phonons</color> responsible for vibrational and rotational energy levels in a substance have much less energy than <color=#3366CC>photons</color>
invoked for the electronic energy transfer. Thus, because vibrational and rotational energy levels are more closely
spaced than electronic energy levels, heat is more easily transferred between substances relative to light or other forms
of electronic energy. For example, <color=#3366CC>ultraviolet</color> electromagnetic radiation is not transferred with as much efficacy from
one substance to another as thermal or electrical energy.
The existence of characteristic energy levels for different <color=#3366CC>chemical substances</color> is useful for their identification by the

analysis of <color=#3366CC>spectral lines</color>. Different kinds of spectra are often used in chemical <color=#3366CC>spectroscopy</color>, e.g. <color=#3366CC>IR</color>, <color=#3366CC>microwave</color>, <color=#3366CC>NMR</color>,
<color=#3366CC>ESR</color>, etc. Spectroscopy is also used to identify the composition of remote objects – like stars and distant galaxies – by
analyzing their radiation spectra.
The term <color=#3366CC>chemical energy</color> is often used to indicate the potential of a chemical substance to undergo a transformation
through a <color=#3366CC>chemical reaction</color> or to transform other chemical substances.
Reaction
When a chemical substance is transformed as a result of its interaction with another substance or with energy, a
chemical reaction is said to have occurred. A chemical reaction is therefore a concept related to the "reaction" of a
substance when it comes in close contact with another, whether as a mixture or a <color=#3366CC>solution</color>; exposure to some form of
energy, or both. It results in some energy exchange between the constituents of the reaction as well as with the system
environment, which may be designed vessels—often <color=#3366CC>laboratory glassware</color>.
Chemical reactions can result in the formation or <color=#3366CC>dissociation</color> of molecules, that is, molecules breaking apart to form
two or more molecules or rearrangement of atoms within or across molecules. Chemical reactions usually involve the
making or breaking of chemical bonds. <color=#3366CC>Oxidation, reduction</color>, dissociation, acid–base neutralization and molecular
<color=#3366CC>rearrangement</color> are some examples of common chemical reactions.
A chemical reaction can be symbolically depicted through a <color=#3366CC>chemical equation</color>. While in a non-nuclear chemical
reaction the number and kind of atoms on both sides of the equation are equal, for a nuclear reaction this holds true
only for the nuclear particles viz. protons and neutrons.
The sequence of steps in which the reorganization of chemical bonds may be taking place in the course of a chemical
reaction is called its <color=#3366CC>mechanism</color>. A chemical reaction can be envisioned to take place in a number of steps, each of
which may have a different speed. Many <color=#3366CC>reaction intermediates</color> with variable stability can thus be envisaged during the
course of a reaction. Reaction mechanisms are proposed to explain the <color=#3366CC>kinetics</color> and the relative product mix of a
reaction. Many <color=#3366CC>physical chemists</color> specialize in exploring and proposing the mechanisms of various chemical reactions.
Several empirical rules, like the Woodward–Hoffmann rules often come in handy while proposing a mechanism for a
chemical reaction.
According to the <color=#3366CC>IUPAC</color> gold book, a chemical reaction is "a process that results in the interconversion of chemical
species." Accordingly, a chemical reaction may be an <color=#3366CC>elementary reaction</color> or a <color=#3366CC>stepwise reaction</color>. An additional caveat
is made, in that this definition includes cases where the <color=#3366CC>interconversion of conformers</color> is experimentally observable.
Such detectable chemical reactions normally involve sets of molecular entities as indicated by this definition, but it is
often conceptually convenient to use the term also for changes involving single molecular entities (i.e. 'microscopic
chemical events').
Ions and salts
An ion is a charged species, an atom or a molecule, that has lost or gained one or more electrons. When an atom loses
an electron and thus has more protons than electrons, the atom is a positively charged ion or <color=#3366CC>cation</color>. When an atom
gains an electron and thus has more electrons than protons, the atom is a negatively charged ion or <color=#3366CC>anion</color>. Cations and
anions can form a crystalline lattice of neutral <color=#3366CC>salts</color>, such as the Na+ and Cl ions forming <color=#3366CC>sodium chloride</color>, or NaCl.

Examples of <color=#3366CC>polyatomic ions</color> that do not split up during <color=#3366CC>acid–base reactions</color> are <color=#3366CC>hydroxide</color> (OH) and <color=#3366CC>phosphate</color> (PO43).
<color=#3366CC>Plasma</color> is composed of gaseous matter that has been completely ionized, usually through high temperature.
Acidity and basicity
A substance can often be classified as an <color=#3366CC>acid</color> or a <color=#3366CC>base</color>. There are several different theories which explain acid–base
behavior. The simplest is <color=#3366CC>Arrhenius theory</color>, which states that an acid is a substance that produces <color=#3366CC>hydronium ions</color>
when it is dissolved in water, and a base is one that produces <color=#3366CC>hydroxide ions</color> when dissolved in water. According to
<color=#3366CC>Brønsted–Lowry acid–base theory</color>, acids are substances that donate a positive <color=#3366CC>hydrogen</color> <color=#3366CC>ion</color> to another substance in a
chemical reaction; by extension, a base is the substance which receives that hydrogen ion.
A third common theory is <color=#3366CC>Lewis acid–base theory</color>, which is based on the formation of new chemical bonds. Lewis
theory explains that an acid is a substance which is capable of accepting a pair of electrons from another substance
during the process of bond formation, while a base is a substance which can provide a pair of electrons to form a new
bond. There are several other ways in which a substance may be classified as an acid or a base, as is evident in the
history of this concept.
Acid strength is commonly measured by two methods. One measurement, based on the Arrhenius definition of acidity,
is <color=#3366CC>pH</color>, which is a measurement of the hydronium ion concentration in a solution, as expressed on a negative <color=#3366CC>logarithmic</color>
scale. Thus, solutions that have a low pH have a high hydronium ion concentration and can be said to be more acidic.
The other measurement, based on the Brønsted–Lowry definition, is the <color=#3366CC>acid dissociation constant</color> (Ka), which
measures the relative ability of a substance to act as an acid under the Brønsted–Lowry definition of an acid. That is,
substances with a higher Ka are more likely to donate hydrogen ions in chemical reactions than those with lower Ka
values.
Redox
Redox (reduction-oxidation) reactions include all <color=#3366CC>chemical reactions</color> in which atoms have their <color=#3366CC>oxidation state</color> changed
by either gaining electrons (reduction) or losing electrons (oxidation). Substances that have the ability to oxidize other
substances are said to be oxidative and are known as <color=#3366CC>oxidizing agents</color>, oxidants or oxidizers. An oxidant removes
electrons from another substance. Similarly, substances that have the ability to reduce other substances are said to be
reductive and are known as <color=#3366CC>reducing agents</color>, reductants, or reducers.
A reductant transfers electrons to another substance and is thus oxidized itself. And because it "donates" electrons it is
also called an electron donor. Oxidation and reduction properly refer to a change in oxidation number—the actual
transfer of electrons may never occur. Thus, oxidation is better defined as an increase in <color=#3366CC>oxidation number</color>, and
reduction as a decrease in oxidation number.
Equilibrium
Although the concept of <color=#3366CC>equilibrium</color> is widely used across sciences, in the context of chemistry, it arises whenever a
number of different states of the chemical composition are possible, as for example, in a mixture of several chemical
compounds that can react with one another, or when a substance can be present in more than one kind of phase.
A system of chemical substances at equilibrium, even though having an unchanging composition, is most often not
<color=#3366CC>static</color>; molecules of the substances continue to react with one another thus giving rise to a dynamic equilibrium. Thus
the concept describes the state in which the parameters such as chemical composition remain unchanged over time.
Chemical laws
Chemical reactions are governed by certain laws, which have become fundamental concepts in chemistry. Some of
them are:
• Avogadro's law
• <color=#3366CC>Beer–Lambert law</color>
• <color=#3366CC>Boyle's law</color> (1662, relating pressure and volume)
• Charles's law (1787, relating volume and temperature)
• Dalton's law (1803, law of partial pressures)
• Fick's laws of diffusion
• Gay-Lussac's law (1809, relating pressure and temperature)
• <color=#3366CC>Ideal gas law</color>
• <color=#3366CC>Le Chatelier's principle</color>
• Henry's law
• <color=#3366CC>Hess's law</color>

• <color=#3366CC>Law of conservation of energy</color> leads to the important concepts of <color=#3366CC>equilibrium</color>, <color=#3366CC>thermodynamics</color>, and <color=#3366CC>kinetics</color>.
• <color=#3366CC>Law of conservation of mass</color> continues to be conserved in isolated systems, even in modern physics. However,
<color=#3366CC>special relativity</color> shows that due to <color=#3366CC>mass–energy equivalence</color>, whenever non-material "energy" (heat, light, kinetic
energy) is removed from a non-isolated system, some mass will be lost with it. High energy losses result in loss of
weighable amounts of mass, an important topic in <color=#3366CC>nuclear chemistry</color>.
• <color=#3366CC>Law of definite proportions</color>, although in many systems (notably biomacromolecules and minerals) the ratios tend to
require large numbers, and are frequently represented as a fraction.
• Raoult's law
History
The <color=#3366CC>history of chemistry</color> spans a period from the ancient past to the present. Since several millennia BC, civilizations
were using technologies that would eventually form the basis of the various branches of chemistry. Examples include
extracting <color=#3366CC>metals</color> from <color=#3366CC>ores</color>, making pottery and glazes, fermenting beer and wine, extracting chemicals from plants for
medicine and perfume, rendering fat into <color=#3366CC>soap</color>, making <color=#3366CC>glass</color>, and making <color=#3366CC>alloys</color> like <color=#3366CC>bronze</color>.
Chemistry was preceded by its protoscience, <color=#3366CC>alchemy</color>, which operated a non-scientific approach to understanding the
constituents of matter and their interactions. Despite being unsuccessful in explaining the nature of matter and its
transformations, alchemists set the stage for modern chemistry by performing experiments and recording the results.
<color=#3366CC>Robert Boyle</color>, although skeptical of elements and convinced of alchemy, played a key part in elevating the "sacred art"
as an independent, fundamental and philosophical discipline in his work The Sceptical Chymist (1661).
While both alchemy and chemistry are concerned with matter and its transformations, the crucial difference was given
by the <color=#3366CC>scientific method</color> that <color=#3366CC>chemists</color> employed in their work. Chemistry, as a body of knowledge distinct from
alchemy, became an established science with the work of <color=#3366CC>Antoine Lavoisier</color>, who developed a law of <color=#3366CC>conservation of</color>
<color=#3366CC>mass</color> that demanded careful measurement and quantitative observations of chemical phenomena. The history of
chemistry afterwards is intertwined with the <color=#3366CC>history of thermodynamics</color>, especially through the work of <color=#3366CC>Willard Gibbs</color>.
Definition
The definition of chemistry has changed over time, as new discoveries and theories add to the functionality of the
science. The term "chymistry", in the view of noted scientist <color=#3366CC>Robert Boyle</color> in 1661, meant the subject of the material
principles of mixed bodies. In 1663, the chemist Christopher Glaser described "chymistry" as a scientific art, by which
one learns to dissolve bodies, and draw from them the different substances on their composition, and how to unite
them again, and exalt them to a higher perfection.
The 1730 definition of the word "chemistry", as used by Georg Ernst Stahl, meant the art of resolving mixed,
compound, or aggregate bodies into their principles; and of composing such bodies from those principles. In 1837,
Jean-Baptiste Dumas considered the word "chemistry" to refer to the science concerned with the laws and effects of
molecular forces. This definition further evolved until, in 1947, it came to mean the science of substances: their
structure, their properties, and the reactions that change them into other substances—a characterization accepted by
<color=#3366CC>Linus Pauling</color>. More recently, in 1998, Professor Raymond Chang broadened the definition of "chemistry" to mean the
study of matter and the changes it undergoes.
Background
Early civilizations, such as the <color=#3366CC>Egyptians</color>, <color=#3366CC>Babylonians</color>, and Indians, amassed practical knowledge concerning the arts
of metallurgy, pottery and dyes, but did not develop a systematic theory.
A basic chemical hypothesis first emerged in <color=#3366CC>Classical Greece</color> with the theory of <color=#3366CC>four elements</color> as propounded
definitively by <color=#3366CC>Aristotle</color> stating that fire, air, earth and water were the fundamental elements from which everything is
formed as a combination. <color=#3366CC>Greek</color> <color=#3366CC>atomism</color> dates back to 440 BC, arising in works by philosophers such as <color=#3366CC>Democritus</color>

and <color=#3366CC>Epicurus</color>. In 50 BCE, the <color=#3366CC>Roman</color> philosopher <color=#3366CC>Lucretius</color> expanded upon the theory in his poem <color=#3366CC>De rerum natura</color>
(On The Nature of Things). Unlike modern concepts of science, Greek atomism was purely philosophical in nature, with
little concern for empirical observations and no concern for chemical experiments.
An early form of the idea of <color=#3366CC>conservation of mass</color> is the notion that "Nothing comes from nothing" in <color=#3366CC>Ancient Greek</color>
<color=#3366CC>philosophy</color>, which can be found in <color=#3366CC>Empedocles</color> (approx. 4th century BC): "For it is impossible for anything to come to
be from what is not, and it cannot be brought about or heard of that what is should be utterly destroyed." and <color=#3366CC>Epicurus</color>
(3rd century BC), who, describing the nature of the Universe, wrote that "the totality of things was always such as it is
now, and always will be".
In the <color=#3366CC>Hellenistic world</color> the art of alchemy first proliferated, mingling magic and occultism into the study of natural
substances with the ultimate goal of transmuting elements into <color=#3366CC>gold</color> and discovering the elixir of eternal life. Work,
particularly the development of <color=#3366CC>distillation</color>, continued in the early <color=#3366CC>Byzantine</color> period with the most famous practitioner
being the 4th century Greek-Egyptian <color=#3366CC>Zosimos of Panopolis</color>. Alchemy continued to be developed and practised
throughout the <color=#3366CC>Arab world</color> after the <color=#3366CC>Muslim conquests</color>, and from there, and from the Byzantine remnants, diffused into
medieval and <color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color> Europe through Latin translations.
The Arabic works attributed to <color=#3366CC>Jabir ibn Hayyan</color> introduced a systematic classification of chemical substances, and
provided instructions for deriving an inorganic compound (sal ammoniac or <color=#3366CC>ammonium chloride</color>) from <color=#3366CC>organic</color>
<color=#3366CC>substances</color> (such as plants, blood, and hair) by chemical means. Some Arabic Jabirian works (e.g., the "Book of
Mercy", and the "Book of Seventy") were later translated into Latin under the Latinized name "Geber", and in
13th-century Europe an anonymous writer, usually referred to as pseudo-Geber, started to produce alchemical and
metallurgical writings under this name. Later influential Muslim philosophers, such as <color=#3366CC>Abū al-Rayhān al-Bīrūnī</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Avicenna</color> disputed the theories of alchemy, particularly the theory of the <color=#3366CC>transmutation of metals</color>.
Improvements of the refining of ores and their extractions to smelt metals was widely used source of information for
early chemists in the 16th century, among them <color=#3366CC>Georg Agricola</color> (1494–1555), who published his major work De re
metallica in 1556. His work, describing highly developed and complex processes of mining metal ores and metal
extraction, were the pinnacle of metallurgy during that time. His approach removed all mysticism associated with the
subject, creating the practical base upon which others could and would build. The work describes the many kinds of
furnaces used to smelt ore, and stimulated interest in minerals and their composition. Agricola has been described as
the "father of metallurgy" and the founder of <color=#3366CC>geology</color> as a scientific discipline.
Under the influence of the <color=#3366CC>Scientific Revolution</color> and its new empirical methods propounded by <color=#3366CC>Sir Francis Bacon</color> and
others, a group of chemists at <color=#3366CC>Oxford</color>, <color=#3366CC>Robert Boyle</color>, <color=#3366CC>Robert Hooke</color> and John Mayow began to reshape the old
alchemical traditions into a scientific discipline. Boyle in particular questioned some commonly held chemical theories
and argued for chemical practitioners to be more "philosophical" and less commercially focused in The Sceptical
Chemyst. He formulated <color=#3366CC>Boyle's law</color>, rejected the classical "four elements" and proposed a mechanistic alternative of
atoms and <color=#3366CC>chemical reactions</color> that could be subject to rigorous experiment.
In the following decades, many important discoveries were made, such as the nature of 'air' which was discovered to be
composed of many different gases. The Scottish chemist <color=#3366CC>Joseph Black</color> and the Flemish <color=#3366CC>Jan Baptist van Helmont</color>
discovered <color=#3366CC>carbon dioxide</color>, or what Black called 'fixed air' in 1754; <color=#3366CC>Henry Cavendish</color> discovered <color=#3366CC>hydrogen</color> and
elucidated its properties and <color=#3366CC>Joseph Priestley</color> and, independently, <color=#3366CC>Carl Wilhelm Scheele</color> isolated pure <color=#3366CC>oxygen</color>. The
theory of <color=#3366CC>phlogiston</color> (a substance at the root of all combustion) was propounded by the German Georg Ernst Stahl in
the early 18th century and was only overturned by the end of the century by the French chemist <color=#3366CC>Antoine Lavoisier</color>, the
chemical analogue of Newton in physics. Lavoisier did more than any other to establish the new science on proper
theoretical footing, by elucidating the principle of <color=#3366CC>conservation of mass</color> and developing a new system of chemical
nomenclature used to this day.
English scientist <color=#3366CC>John Dalton</color> proposed the modern <color=#3366CC>theory of atoms</color>; that all substances are composed of indivisible
'atoms' of matter and that different atoms have varying atomic weights.
The development of the electrochemical theory of chemical combinations occurred in the early 19th century as the
result of the work of two scientists in particular, <color=#3366CC>Jöns Jacob Berzelius</color> and <color=#3366CC>Humphry Davy</color>, made possible by the prior
invention of the voltaic pile by <color=#3366CC>Alessandro Volta</color>. Davy discovered nine new elements including the <color=#3366CC>alkali metals</color> by
extracting them from their <color=#3366CC>oxides</color> with electric current.
British William Prout first proposed ordering all the elements by their atomic weight as all atoms had a weight that was
an exact multiple of the atomic weight of hydrogen. J.A.R. Newlands devised an early table of elements, which was
then developed into the modern <color=#3366CC>periodic table</color> of elements in the 1860s by <color=#3366CC>Dmitri Mendeleev</color> and independently by
several other scientists including Julius Lothar Meyer. The inert gases, later called the <color=#3366CC>noble gases</color> were discovered by
<color=#3366CC>William Ramsay</color> in collaboration with <color=#3366CC>Lord Rayleigh</color> at the end of the century, thereby filling in the basic structure of the
table.
Organic chemistry was developed by <color=#3366CC>Justus von Liebig</color> and others, following <color=#3366CC>Friedrich Wöhler</color>'s synthesis of <color=#3366CC>urea</color>.
Other crucial 19th century advances were; an understanding of valence bonding (Edward Frankland in 1852) and the
application of thermodynamics to chemistry (<color=#3366CC>J. W. Gibbs</color> and <color=#3366CC>Svante Arrhenius</color> in the 1870s).
At the turn of the twentieth century the theoretical underpinnings of chemistry were finally understood due to a series of
remarkable discoveries that succeeded in probing and discovering the very nature of the internal structure of atoms. In
1897, <color=#3366CC>J.J. Thomson</color> of the <color=#3366CC>University of Cambridge</color> discovered the <color=#3366CC>electron</color> and soon after the French scientist

<color=#3366CC>Becquerel</color> as well as the couple <color=#3366CC>Pierre</color> and <color=#3366CC>Marie Curie</color> investigated the phenomenon of <color=#3366CC>radioactivity</color>. In a series of
pioneering scattering experiments <color=#3366CC>Ernest Rutherford</color> at the <color=#3366CC>University of Manchester</color> discovered the internal structure
of the atom and the existence of the proton, classified and explained the different types of radioactivity and successfully
transmuted the first element by bombarding <color=#3366CC>nitrogen</color> with <color=#3366CC>alpha particles</color>.
His work on atomic structure was improved on by his students, the Danish physicist <color=#3366CC>Niels Bohr</color>, the Englishman Henry
Moseley and the German <color=#3366CC>Otto Hahn</color>, who went on to father the emerging <color=#3366CC>nuclear chemistry</color> and discovered <color=#3366CC>nuclear</color>

<color=#3366CC>fission</color>. The electronic theory of <color=#3366CC>chemical bonds</color> and <color=#3366CC>molecular orbitals</color> was developed by the American scientists <color=#3366CC>Linus</color>
<color=#3366CC>Pauling</color> and <color=#3366CC>Gilbert N. Lewis</color>.
The year 2011 was declared by the United Nations as the International Year of Chemistry. As one of the United
Nations' many International Year designations, it was an initiative to broaden outreach and public understanding in
chemistry. The year was chosen as the 100th anniversary of <color=#3366CC>Marie Curie</color>'s receipt of the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Several years later, in 2019, the UN declared the International Year of the Periodic Table.
Practice
In the practice of chemistry, pure chemistry is the study of the fundamental principles of chemistry, while applied
chemistry applies that knowledge to develop technology and solve real-world problems.
Subdisciplines
Chemistry is typically divided into several major sub-disciplines. There are also several main cross-disciplinary and
more specialized fields of chemistry.
• <color=#3366CC>Analytical chemistry</color> is the analysis of material samples to gain an understanding of their <color=#3366CC>chemical composition</color> and
structure. Analytical chemistry incorporates standardized experimental methods in chemistry. These methods may
be used in all subdisciplines of chemistry, excluding purely theoretical chemistry.

• <color=#3366CC>Biochemistry</color> is the study of the <color=#3366CC>chemicals</color>, <color=#3366CC>chemical reactions</color> and interactions that occur in living <color=#3366CC>organisms</color>.
Biochemistry is highly interdisciplinary, covering <color=#3366CC>medicinal chemistry</color>, neurochemistry, <color=#3366CC>molecular biology</color>, <color=#3366CC>forensics</color>,
<color=#3366CC>plant science</color> and <color=#3366CC>genetics</color>. Neurochemistry is the study of neurochemicals; including transmitters, peptides,
proteins, lipids, sugars, and nucleic acids; their interactions, and the roles they play in forming, maintaining, and
modifying the nervous system.
• <color=#3366CC>Inorganic chemistry</color> traditionally was the study of metals and minerals, but is mainly concerned with the structure
and behavior of compounds derived from metals and <color=#3366CC>main group elements</color>. The distinction between organic and
inorganic disciplines is not absolute and there is much overlap, most importantly in the sub-discipline of
<color=#3366CC>organometallic chemistry</color>.
• <color=#3366CC>Materials chemistry</color> is the preparation, characterization, and understanding of solid state components or devices
with a useful current or future function. The field is a new breadth of study in graduate programs, and it integrates
elements from all classical areas of chemistry like <color=#3366CC>organic chemistry</color>, <color=#3366CC>inorganic chemistry</color>, and <color=#3366CC>crystallography</color> with
a focus on fundamental issues that are unique to <color=#3366CC>materials</color>. Primary systems of study include the chemistry of
condensed phases (solids, liquids, <color=#3366CC>polymers</color>) and interfaces between different phases.
• <color=#3366CC>Organic chemistry</color> is the study of the structure, properties, composition, mechanisms, and <color=#3366CC>reactions</color> of <color=#3366CC>organic</color>
<color=#3366CC>compounds</color>. An organic compound is defined as any compound based on a carbon skeleton. Organic compounds
can be classified, organized and understood in reactions by their <color=#3366CC>functional groups</color>, unit atoms or molecules that
show characteristic chemical properties in a compound.
• <color=#3366CC>Physical chemistry</color> is the study of the physical and fundamental basis of chemical systems and processes. In
particular, the energetics and dynamics of such systems and processes are of interest to physical chemists.
Important areas of study include <color=#3366CC>chemical thermodynamics</color>, <color=#3366CC>chemical kinetics</color>, <color=#3366CC>electrochemistry</color>, <color=#3366CC>statistical</color>

<color=#3366CC>mechanics</color>, <color=#3366CC>spectroscopy</color>, and more recently, <color=#3366CC>astrochemistry</color>. Physical chemistry has large overlap with <color=#3366CC>molecular</color>
<color=#3366CC>physics</color>. Physical chemistry involves the use of <color=#3366CC>infinitesimal calculus</color> in deriving equations. It is usually associated
with <color=#3366CC>quantum chemistry</color> and theoretical chemistry. Physical chemistry is a distinct discipline from <color=#3366CC>chemical physics</color>,
but again, there is very strong overlap.
• <color=#3366CC>Theoretical chemistry</color> is the study of chemistry via fundamental theoretical reasoning (usually within <color=#3366CC>mathematics</color>
or <color=#3366CC>physics</color>). In particular the application of <color=#3366CC>quantum mechanics</color> to chemistry is called <color=#3366CC>quantum chemistry</color>. Since the
end of the <color=#3366CC>Second World War</color>, the development of computers has allowed a systematic development of
<color=#3366CC>computational chemistry</color>, which is the art of developing and applying <color=#3366CC>computer programs</color> for solving chemical
problems. Theoretical chemistry has large overlap with (theoretical and experimental) <color=#3366CC>condensed matter physics</color>
and <color=#3366CC>molecular physics</color>.
Other subdivisions include <color=#3366CC>electrochemistry</color>, femtochemistry, flavor chemistry, flow chemistry, immunohistochemistry,
<color=#3366CC>hydrogenation chemistry</color>, mathematical chemistry, molecular mechanics, <color=#3366CC>natural product chemistry</color>, <color=#3366CC>organometallic</color>
<color=#3366CC>chemistry</color>, <color=#3366CC>petrochemistry</color>, <color=#3366CC>photochemistry</color>, physical organic chemistry, <color=#3366CC>polymer chemistry</color>, radiochemistry,
sonochemistry, <color=#3366CC>supramolecular chemistry</color>, <color=#3366CC>synthetic chemistry</color>, and many others.
Interdisciplinary

<color=#3366CC>Interdisciplinary</color> fields include <color=#3366CC>agrochemistry</color>, <color=#3366CC>astrochemistry</color> (and <color=#3366CC>cosmochemistry</color>), atmospheric chemistry, <color=#3366CC>chemical</color>

<color=#3366CC>engineering</color>, <color=#3366CC>chemical biology</color>, <color=#3366CC>chemo-informatics</color>, <color=#3366CC>environmental chemistry</color>, <color=#3366CC>geochemistry</color>, <color=#3366CC>green chemistry</color>,

immunochemistry, <color=#3366CC>marine chemistry</color>, <color=#3366CC>materials science</color>, mechanochemistry, <color=#3366CC>medicinal chemistry</color>, <color=#3366CC>molecular biology</color>,

<color=#3366CC>nanotechnology</color>, oenology, <color=#3366CC>pharmacology</color>, phytochemistry, <color=#3366CC>solid-state chemistry</color>, <color=#3366CC>surface science</color>, <color=#3366CC>thermochemistry</color>,
and many others.
Industry

2013 had sales of <color=#3366CC>US$</color>980.5 billion with a profit margin of 10.3%.
